title: Quantity Discrimination in Zebrafish
short: Experimental work on how larval zebrafish discriminate between quantities, and whether they apply learned arithmetic-like rules.
description: This project looks at numerical cognition in larval zebrafish. Quantity discrimination is well documented across animal taxa; whether animals can go further and apply learned rules to new quantities — adding or subtracting according to an abstract symbol — is a harder question.
I developed and refined the paradigms for this work, including a dot-splitting task and a ratio-comparison task in a T-maze, and built the apparatus and visual stimuli used to run them.
researchQuestion: Can larval zebrafish discriminate between quantities, and do their choices follow a ratio rule rather than continuous cues such as surface area?
background: Fish are capable of non-symbolic numerosity cognition: they discriminate larger from smaller shoals, and their accuracy is ratio-dependent, particularly at higher quantities, consistent with an approximate number system.

The complication is that fish also use non-numerical cues — surface area, density and other continuous variables. The behavioral literature disagrees about how much of a fish's apparent numerosity performance is numerical rather than perceptual.

A recent line of work in cichlids and stingrays has shown that fish can learn to associate abstract visual symbols with +1 and –1 operations and then apply those rules correctly to novel quantities. That is proto-arithmetic capacity, and it is what makes this work interesting to pursue.
A review of 15+ studies on ratio and multiplicative cognition, presented to the lab, fed into a publication proposal.
